Ampacity and Voltage-Drop Checks

Calculation Details

MetricValueNote

How this wire size calculator works

The tool compares two constraints: reference ampacity after applying the continuous-load factor and conductor size needed to stay within the entered voltage-drop limit. It recommends the larger conductor produced by those two checks.

design current = noncontinuous amps + 125% x continuous amps

Wire-size example

A 24 A load that is entirely continuous produces 30 A of design current. For a 100 ft, 240 V single-phase copper circuit with a 3% drop target, 10 AWG satisfies the simplified 30 A reference ampacity and keeps estimated voltage drop below the target.

Ampacity is installation-specific

The 60°C and 75°C choices are reference columns, not permission to use a temperature rating. Terminal ratings, insulation, conductor material, ambient temperature, conductor count, cable type, wet locations, and special equipment rules can change the permitted ampacity. Small-conductor overcurrent limits are included conservatively in this planning table.

Voltage-drop check

The voltage-drop calculation uses approximate conductor resistance and actual entered load current. Southwire's professional building wire selector explains that final selection remains subject to current codes, the licensed electrician, and the local authority having jurisdiction.

Frequently asked questions

Why can voltage drop require a larger wire?

A conductor may carry the load safely at a short distance but lose too much voltage over a long run. The final recommendation uses whichever requirement produces the larger size.

Can I size service conductors with this?

No. Services, feeders, motors, HVAC, EV charging, and other equipment can have additional rules. Use project-specific engineering and code calculations.

Should continuous load exceed total load?

No. The calculator caps the continuous portion at the entered total load.
